content: Peonidin is a type of anthocyanidin, which is a class of compounds responsible for pigmentation in plants. It is a primary plant pigment that imparts purplish-red hues to flowers such as peonies and roses, from which its name is derived. Additionally, peonidin is found in certain blue flowers, such as the morning glory. Like most anthocyanidins, peonidin is sensitive to pH changes. Its color shifts from red to blue as the pH increases. This phenomenon occurs because anthocyanidins are highly conjugated chromophores, meaning their molecular structure contains a system of alternating double bonds. When the pH changes, the degree of conjugation is altered, which in turn changes the wavelength of light absorbed by the molecule. At a neutral pH, most anthocyanidins become colorless. At higher pH levels, peonidin becomes a deep blue. Unlike many other anthocyanidins, peonidin is stable at higher pH levels and has even been isolated as a blue pigment from the Heavenly Blue morning glory (Ipomoea tricolor Cav cv). Due to its unusual color stability, a buffered, acylated form of peonidin has been patented for use as a food coloring agent. Peonidin has demonstrated significant inhibitory and pro-apoptotic effects on cancer cells in vitro, particularly against metastatic human breast cancer cells. However, there is considerable uncertainty regarding the ability of anthocyanidins, including peonidin, to penetrate and remain within human cells in vivo, as they are rapidly eliminated from the human body. The richest dietary source of peonidin is raw cranberries, which contain approximately 42 mg per 100 g of fruit. Other fruits, such as blueberries, plums, grapes, and cherries, also contain notable amounts of peonidin, ranging from 5 to 12 mg per 100 g. However, only fresh fruit has been shown to contain significant levels of peonidin; frozen blueberries, for example, contain almost none. Peonidin has also been isolated from raw black rice and black bananas. The higher levels of peonidin in fresh fruit align with the general principle that more natural, unprocessed fruits are healthier. Specifically, the phenolic compound content in cranberries has been found to inversely correlate with fruit size and crop yield, suggesting that smaller, less cultivated fruits may be richer in beneficial compounds.
